issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (and specify a static final Stock stock in SealSaloon), but the provided template implements an 'Inventory' class with the required stock functionality while src/de/tum/cit/ase/Stock.java is empty. The solution also uses Inventory (static final Inventory stock). This mismatch between 'Stock' and 'Inventory' is a structural naming/type inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to use or implement and prevents following the specification as written.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the name and type for the shared stock consistent across all artifacts. Either: (A) Rename the Inventory class (and its file) to Stock throughout the template and solution and remove/replace the empty Stock.java file, or (B) Update the problem statement and UML to reference Inventory instead of Stock. Ensure SealSaloon uses the same static final type as declared in the chosen class (Stock or Inventory) so students have a single consistent class to use.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Stock class (and expect a static final Stock stock in SealSaloon), but the provided template and the reference solution implement this concept as an Inventory class. Additionally, a (mostly empty) Stock.java file exists in the template/solution which increases confusion. This mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) forces students to map the problem description to a differently named implementation and may cause them to search for or attempt to implement a Stock class that is not used, increasing extraneous cognitive load.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier across artifacts. Either (A) rename the Inventory class (and its file) to Stock and update all references (SealSaloon and documentation) accordingly, removing or implementing Stock.java consistently; or (B) update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Ensure a single canonical name (Stock or Inventory) is used in the problem statement, template, and solution.
